item.title: The 2026 manufacturing trust gap, and one weekly fix
item.content:encoded:
More systems will not fix it. The trust gap is about who owns the exception, reconciles the signal, and turns output into a decision before reality has already changed.
 

By Bill Murphy  ·  Powered by Colony Spark

THE OPERATIONS
BRIEF

 

ISSUE #13  ·  MAY 14, 2026
 
 

Hi there,

Operators are not short on data this year. They are short on trust in what their systems are telling them.

This issue is about the gap between what the report says and what is actually happening: why it has gotten more expensive in 2026, what it looks like when a team closes it, and the system your team can run starting Monday.

— Bill
 

THE SHIFT

The System Trust Gap.

More dashboards will not fix it. Exception ownership will.

Manufacturers are not short on software. They are short on trusted operating signal.

The factory has ERP. Finance has reconciliation workflows. Supervisors have reports. Sales and customer service have CRM notes, inboxes, and dashboards. Each system produces a version of reality, and operators still have to answer the same old question every week: is this number safe enough to act on?

That question is more expensive in 2026 because the operating environment has compressed the time between signal and consequence. A material shortage discovered after the plan is locked triggers premium freight, production rescheduling, margin leakage, customer escalations, and another round of manual follow-up. A dashboard that shows inventory but cannot explain whether the plant can actually execute is not a decision system. It is another place to check.

The pattern is not "bad data" in the abstract. It is exception ownership. When the system says one thing and the floor says another, who owns the discrepancy? Who confirms the signal? Who updates the record? Who tells purchasing, production, finance, and the customer-facing team what changed? If that ownership is unclear, the team quietly rebuilds the business in spreadsheets, side conversations, and Friday afternoon panic calls.

Three 2026 signals that make the gap visible

· 75% of supply plan failures happen at the factory execution stage, not in the planning model. 73% say their ERP can show required materials but cannot prevent execution failures. 93% report difficulty getting ERP visibility into actual execution outcomes (LeanDNA via CFOtech).

· 64% of manufacturers spend 10%+ of their manufacturing budget reacting to disruption: premium freight, emergency sourcing, last-minute schedule changes. 84% hit inventory shortages multiple times last year. 80%+ are also carrying excess inventory at the same time.

· Plants generating 50–100+ weekly reports are absorbing 25–75 supervisor hours/week on manual compilation, with 1–3% transcription error rates and reports arriving 4–8 hours old (iFactory 2026 reporting guide).

The operating question for 2026 is not "how many reports do we have." It is "which reports are allowed to trigger action, and who is accountable when the report is wrong."

The gap is not "do we have the data." The gap is "does anyone own the exception, reconcile the signal, update the record, and turn system output into a decision before trust erodes."
 

FROM THE FLOOR

Trust is not a reporting preference.
It is execution capacity.

Ryan Hosmer, Light Composites, on closing the gap between system record and floor reality

Light Composites is a 55-person aerospace and medical composites manufacturer in San Diego. Before they rebuilt their operating layer, the business ran on paper and Excel. GM Andy Hosmer described it plainly: "We were doing everything on a paper system and Excel spreadsheets. Somehow, we were able to hold it all together, but we could not scale." Shortages were being discovered through frantic vendor calls, not the system.

"Recently, we did an inventory check, and we were within 97 to 98% of what the system says we should have. Eliminating stockouts has been a godsend. Because if you have the order but cannot ship it, you are not going to make money."

Ryan Hosmer

CEO, Light Composites  ·  Manufacturing.net

This is the trust gap in operator language. The breakthrough was not adding a dashboard. It was getting the system record close enough to physical reality that the team could ship from it, forecast from it, trace quality through it, and plan capacity against it. Hosmer also noted the second-order effect: "We have a high degree of confidence that the material it says went into it actually did, and that the labor recorded actually happened."

When the system record matches the floor, the team stops working around it. That is what closing the trust gap actually buys you: not better reporting, but the ability to act on what the system says.

The takeaway

98% inventory accuracy is not the headline metric. The headline is that the team now trusts the system enough to make decisions from it instead of working around it. Trust is not a soft outcome. It is the difference between shipping the order and missing the order.

Note: Light Composites story originally published by their software vendor and republished by Manufacturing.net. The quotes are from the operator about their own business, but the case study isn't independent reporting. Worth treating as directional, not benchmark.
 

THE STACK

The Weekly Customer Health Pulse.

One owner for the signals your systems already have.

Not a dashboard someone has to remember to check. A decision packet with named owners, trigger reasons, recommended actions, and write-backs.

Most customer risk does not appear all at once. It leaks through small signals that live in separate systems. A support ticket stays open longer than usual. A reorder comes in late. A payment slips from 31 days to 47 days. A buyer who normally answers same day goes quiet.

The Weekly Customer Health Pulse is an agentic workflow that pulls those signals into one weekly exception list, and updates the system of record so the loop closes.

What it pulls

· Support tickets: open count by account, aging by severity, reopened tickets, escalations, SLA misses

· Order behavior: order frequency vs. 13-week and 52-week baselines, missed reorder windows, partial shipments, backorders, canceled lines

· Payment timing: DSO by account, change vs. normal behavior, past due amount, short-pay or dispute notes

· Communication pattern: days since last meaningful touch, unanswered emails, negative sentiment in notes, new stakeholders appearing in threads, mentions of competitor, rebid, or vendor review

Trigger logic

· Red: severe escalation + missed reorder window + no customer reply in 7 days

· Red: payment delay 15+ days beyond account norm + unresolved billing or delivery dispute

· Yellow: order frequency down 25%+ from 13-week baseline + support tickets 2x baseline

· Yellow: expected reorder missed 10 business days + buyer communication volume down 50%

· Watch: new stakeholder on 3+ threads while order volume or payment timing is slipping

Weekly output, Monday morning

1. Top 10 accounts needing attention: name, status, owner, trigger reason, evidence, recommended action, deadline

2. Newly deteriorating accounts: what changed, and whether it's operational, financial, relationship, or mixed

3. Recovery accounts: which signal normalized, whether records were updated

4. Write-back queue: CRM tasks created, account status updated, AR notes added, owners notified

The write-back queue is the trust layer. If the agent only summarizes risk, the team gets another report. If it updates the system of record and creates owner-specific tasks, the business gets a cleaner operating loop. That is the difference between this and the dashboards already sitting unread.

Path 1: Internal build

Start with exports from help desk, ERP, accounting, CRM, and email metadata. Define 8–12 triggers. Run it manually for 30 days before automating any write-backs. The first win is not the AI. It is agreement on which signals count and who owns each exception.

Path 2: ERP or partner

If customer, order, AR, and support data already live in the ERP ecosystem, build the pulse there. Use native alerts where possible, then add an agent layer for cross-system reasoning and task creation.

The operating question isn't how many reports you have. It's which reports are allowed to trigger action, and who is accountable when the report is wrong.

item.title: When is the last time your ERP told you something you didn't already know?
item.content:encoded:
The gap is not who has AI. It's who is still running it six months after they turned it on. The four questions every leadership team should be asking the ERP every ninety days.
‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ 
 

THE OPERATIONS
BRIEF
 

THE ERP VALUE GAP

By Bill Murphy  ·  Powered by Colony Spark
 
 

Hi there,

The gap widening across mid-market manufacturing and distribution right now is not who bought the most sophisticated ERP. It is who is still actively running it six months after the consultant left.

This issue is about that gap. Why it compounds, where it shows up, and the operating rhythm leadership teams can build now to close it before the next quarter of margin drift.

— Bill

 

THE SHIFT

The gap is not who has AI.

It is who is still running it six months after they turned it on.

The pattern is consistent across manufacturing and distribution right now. A company buys an ERP. They go through the implementation. The consultant team runs the project, trains the team, and gets everything live. Metrics improve. The project closes.

Then the consultant leaves. The team goes back to running the business. The system runs exactly as configured, recording every transaction, processing every order, doing exactly what it was set up to do the day the project ended.

Twelve months later, products have been added. Customers have shifted their buying patterns. Tariffs have restructured the cost stack. A supplier that wasn't a concern before now represents 40% of spend in a tariff-exposed category. The system is still running. It just doesn't know any of that.

This is not a technology problem. It is not an implementation problem. It is a discipline problem.

The companies pulling ahead are not the ones that bought the most sophisticated ERP. They are the ones still actively running it: connecting it to AI, measuring what's changed since the last configuration, asking the system what it knows that the leadership team hasn't asked yet.

Three things shifting at the same time

1. The tools are now accessible. Oracle launched the NetSuite AI Connector Service in April 2026, enabling manufacturers and distributors to connect Claude, GPT, and other AI models directly into live ERP data via the Model Context Protocol. Role-based access controls. Over 100 prompt templates. Bring your own AI model.

2. The investment is happening, but the value isn't following. Rockwell Automation's State of Smart Manufacturing report found that 95% of manufacturing leaders have invested or plan to invest in AI in the next five years. The spend is real. The discipline isn't.

3. The margin environment has no patience for systems that drift. A static ERP that isn't actively connected to current operating reality is annoying in a normal market. With tariffs moving, freight unpredictable, and customer mix shifting, it is expensive. The ERP knows. Most leadership teams never ask.

The advantage in 2026 is not who has the best AI tool. It is who is still running the tools they already have, every quarter, connected to the operating decisions that actually matter.

 

FROM THE FLOOR

Owning the tool is not
the same as orchestrating it.

Ryan Hawk, PwC, on what compounds after deployment

Ryan Hawk, global and U.S. industrials and services leader at PwC, framed the operating reality cleanly in a March Manufacturing Dive interview.

"As automation becomes ubiquitous, the advantage shifts from who has tools to who can orchestrate them across the enterprise."

Ryan Hawk

Global & U.S. Industrials and Services Leader, PwC  ·  Manufacturing Dive, March 4, 2026

Hawk's point is not about technology selection. It is about what shows up after deployment. PwC's analysis found that automation in manufacturing is expected to more than double by 2030. The companies that will compound the value of that automation are the ones that can connect it to how they actually operate. Not just turn it on.

The research tracked a consistent pattern: manufacturers who treat AI as a deployment project and move on get a fraction of the value that manufacturers treating it as an operating discipline extract over the same period.

The framing translates directly to the ERP environment most mid-market manufacturers and distributors are sitting in right now. Most bought the tools. Most went live. Most stopped there. The orchestration gap is not abstract. It is the distance between a system that accurately records every transaction and a system that the leadership team actively uses to make decisions every quarter. Most ERP systems don't degrade. They just don't get asked anything new.

The question worth sitting with

When is the last time your ERP told you something you didn't already know? Every quarter that passes without someone connecting current operating reality to the system's data model is another quarter where margin pressure, supplier concentration, customer attrition, and inventory drift accumulate without showing up in a conversation that can do something about them.
 

THE STACK

The Quarterly ERP Health Snapshot.

A working pattern for closing the gap.

Not a dashboard. A dashboard shows what is happening. A snapshot connects what is happening to what it means for the next decision.

The pattern we keep seeing across mid-market operators is the same. The system was working. The team was busy. But nobody was asking the ERP the right questions every quarter. Margin was drifting. Supplier concentration was building. Customer mix was shifting. The data was there. The operating rhythm was not.

A Quarterly ERP Health Snapshot sits between the ERP and the leadership team. It connects to live ERP transaction data, prior quarter benchmarks, and supplier pricing history. The output is a brief, not raw data: a short read that surfaces what changed since last quarter and one decision worth making about it. The framing below is what the operators we have seen run this well actually receive.

What the leadership team receives every quarter

Margin drift report. Where margin eroded since last quarter and what drove it. Price change, cost increase, customer mix shift, volume decline. Specific, not aggregate.

Inventory health check. Slow-moving SKUs with capital tied up. Out-of-stock risk in active product lines. Over-procurement flags where seasonal patterns were missed.

Customer concentration watch. Which accounts grew, which shrank, and what the revenue mix looks like now versus six months ago. The ERP has the data. The snapshot surfaces the pattern.

Supplier exposure summary. Which suppliers represent the highest pricing leverage based on actual order history and category concentration. In this tariff environment, this is the analysis the CFO should see every quarter.

Plus: One Decision

The single highest-priority operating question the data is raising for the leadership team. A snapshot that only describes the past is a report. One that surfaces the next decision is an operating tool.

Path 1: Through your ERP partner

Add a quarterly intelligence engagement on top of the system you already paid to implement. Most ERP partners can scope this as a recurring layer of post-implementation work; some are doing it already.

Path 2: Build it internally

Use the AI tools now connected directly into NetSuite, Acumatica, and other cloud ERPs through the new MCP integration layer. The capability is no longer the constraint. The discipline of running it every quarter is.

The leadership teams asking the ERP four hard questions every ninety days are the ones who will compound through this margin environment. The ones still treating go-live as the finish line will keep paying for a system that runs accurately and tells them nothing. Build the rhythm now, while you still have options.

Volatility is no longer the story. Readiness is. The advantage is not prediction, it is response time. Here is what that looks like at ground level.

FROM COLONY SPARK

THE OPERATIONS
BRIEF
 

ISSUE #7  · MAY 1, 2026
 
 

Hi there,

Volatility is no longer the story. Readiness is.

This issue is about the split we are watching in the market right now. On one side, companies still treating each disruption as a one-off fire drill. On the other, companies building the operating muscle to respond before the margin damage shows up in the P&L. Here is what that looks like, where it is showing up on the floor, and the system your team can build this week.

 

THE SHIFT

From Reactive to Ready.

The operators pulling ahead are not outguessing tariff chaos. They are building response systems.

The shift is not that volatility is back. Volatility is the operating environment now.

Tariffs move. Input costs jump. Court rulings change refund exposure. Suppliers absorb some costs, pass through others, and wait for policy to settle. The old response was to gather the leadership team after the shock hit and ask, "What do we do now?"

That is too slow.

What we are seeing now is a split between companies still treating each disruption as a one-off fire drill, and companies building the operating muscle to respond before the margin damage shows up in the P&L. The winners are not betting on the right tariff opinion. They are building readiness into the business.

What readiness actually looks like

· Clean data foundation across item, supplier, landed cost, and customer records

· Scenario models that show margin exposure before price changes hit

· Communication workflows that move suppliers and customers in days, not weeks

· Early warning reporting that flags risk in time for commercial, finance, and ops to act together

· Documented playbooks for when tariffs, freight, commodity costs, or lead times move again

The question for operators is no longer, "Can we predict the next disruption?" The better question is, "How fast can we turn new information into a decision?"

The numbers operators are responding to

· ISM Prices Index hit 78.3% in March, up 7.8 points from February, with price increases across 17 of 18 manufacturing industries (ISM March 2026 PMI)

· 48% of CEOs are actively modeling and deploying tariff mitigation strategies, and 41% are using AI to manage trade compliance (KPMG 2026 CEO Outlook Pulse)

· $127 billion in tariff refunds now processing electronically through CBP's CAPE system, with about 56,497 importers registered as of April 9 (Supply Chain Dive)

Those KPMG figures are not "wait and see" numbers. They are companies that decided their response system matters more than their forecast accuracy. And on the recovery side, the importers documenting their exposure cleanly are the ones positioned to recover money. The ones running everything through one person's head are still trying to reconstruct what they paid.

The companies that win this year will not be the ones with the best tariff take. They will be the ones with the fastest path from signal to decision.

 

FROM THE FLOOR

The planning window
has collapsed.

Jason Wong, Paking Duck, on stacked disruption in packaging

Jason Wong, founder and CEO of Paking Duck, gave Supply Chain Dive a sentence that sounds like a lot of operators are feeling right now but struggling to articulate.

"These black swan events keep coming at us. We just don't have time to prepare."

Jason Wong

Founder & CEO, Paking Duck  ·  Supply Chain Dive, April 13, 2026

Wong is describing the reality many operators are living through. Not one disruption, but stacked disruptions that keep compressing the planning window.

Packaging companies and their customers are dealing with tariffs, commodity shifts, geopolitical conflict, supplier constraints, and customer price sensitivity all at once. Domestic sourcing is not always viable. Stockpiling only solves part of the problem. Passing costs through can damage demand.

That is why the quote lands. It is not just frustration. It is an operating diagnosis.

The diagnosis

The answer is not perfect forecasting. Nobody has that. The answer is reducing reaction time: knowing what changed, who is affected, what margin is at risk, what commitments already exist, and what decision has to be made next.
 

THE STACK

The Post-Call Intelligence Agent.

What we are building, and what it is doing.

Not a meeting summary bot. That is too small. A context engine for the account, project, supplier, or internal initiative.

This is the system we have been building at Colony Spark for B2B teams in the $2–10M range, and it is the most direct answer I have found to the reaction-time problem in The Shift.

A Post-Call Intelligence Agent sits between every important conversation and the next operating decision. We feed it what was said, what was promised, and what is at risk, and it turns that into the next action automatically. Less tribal knowledge stuck in someone's inbox. Faster path from signal to decision.

What we feed it

· Call transcripts from Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, or phone notes

· CRM account record and open opportunities

· Last week's account brief or project brief

· Open support tickets, implementation blockers, or delivery risks

· Prior commitments made by either side

· Pricing, renewal, inventory, or margin notes where relevant

· Internal Slack threads or project updates tied to the account

What lands in the team's inbox Monday

A one-page account pulse, in inbox or Slack, with:

· Commitments made: who promised what, by when

· Risks flagged: supplier delay, tariff exposure, customer volume change, unresolved ticket, pricing pressure

· Decision needed: what requires leadership, finance, ops, or sales input

· Next best action: what should happen before the next customer or supplier conversation

· Context carried forward: last stated priority, prior objection, open blocker, commercial impact

· Next brief generated: a ready-to-use prep note for the next meeting

The operator no longer has to decide who is going to read the notes, remember the promise, update the CRM, chase the project tracker, or piece together what changed since the last conversation. The system does the first pass automatically, and routes the exceptions to the right person.

What we are seeing on the accounts running this: fewer dropped follow-ups, faster pattern recognition when the same concern shows up across customers or suppliers, and a real reduction in the quiet tax of reconstructing context every Monday morning. In a stable market, that tax is annoying. In this market, it is expensive. If tariffs change, a supplier slips, a customer cuts volume, or a margin assumption moves, the team needs to connect today's conversation to last week's decision and next week's action without digging through five systems.

For operators

Fewer missed follow-ups. Fewer handoff errors. Less tribal knowledge trapped in inboxes. Faster pattern recognition when the same concern starts showing up across accounts or suppliers, before the damage is done.

For teams selling into manufacturers and distributors

Reps stop showing up vague. They walk in knowing the customer's last stated priority, the unresolved issue, the promised follow-up, and the operating context around the account. That changes the quality of the conversation immediately.

The edge is not more activity. The edge is memory inside the workflow — a system that makes sure the business can remember, decide, and act faster than the disruption cycle.

item.title: The real cost of the Chief Everything Officer
item.content:encoded:
The operators getting ahead aren't predicting better. They built systems so the business responds without waiting on one person. Here's what that looks like — and the tool your team can deploy this week.
‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ 
 
BY BILL MURPHY

THE OPERATIONS
BRIEF
 

ISSUE #6  · APRIL, 2026
 
 

Hi there,

The companies pulling ahead right now are not the ones with better forecasts. They are the ones that stopped depending on one person to hold the whole operation together.

This issue is about that difference — why the founder bottleneck is now a market response problem, what it looks like on the floor, and the one system your team can build this week to stop depending on memory.

 

THE SHIFT

The Founder Bottleneck is now
a market response problem.

Why holding tighter in volatility is exactly backward

Every operator I talk to right now is dealing with some version of the same problem. Tariffs are stacking. Input costs are moving. Supply chains are getting rearranged on short notice. And the instinct — for most founders, most leadership teams — is to hold tighter. Control more. Make more decisions yourself.

That instinct is exactly backward.

I wrote about this recently in a piece on the founder bottleneck — the pattern where everything in a company still runs through one person. The revenue flattens. The team waits for approvals. The sales cycle stretches because no one else can close the deal. The skills that built the company to $3M are the same ones preventing it from reaching $10M.

One symptom I flag in that piece: when your positioning is built entirely around the founder's personal credibility, every deal collapses into a vendor comparison the moment you're not in the room. If that's where deals are dying for you, the Revenue Messaging Audit is where we start with every client — it shows you exactly why you're stuck there, and what the path to strategic partner positioning looks like.

That framing is about growth ceilings. But the same dynamic is showing up right now in how companies respond to market volatility.

The numbers operators are responding to

· ISM Prices Index hit 78.3% in March — up 7.8 points from February, with price increases across 17 of 18 sectors tracked

· 48% of organizations are actively modeling and deploying tariff mitigation strategies (KPMG 2026 CEO Outlook)

· 41% are deploying AI to manage trade compliance

· $127 billion in tariff returns now being processed electronically by CBP

When one person holds all the context — the supplier relationships, the pricing logic, the customer commitments — the business can only react as fast as that person's calendar allows. And in a market moving this fast, "as fast as one person's calendar" is not fast enough.

The operators getting ahead are doing something different. They are building systems that carry context forward without depending on any single person to hold it. Documentation discipline. Decision frameworks that let the team act without waiting. Intelligence layers that surface the right information before someone has to go looking for it.

Those KPMG numbers are not "wait and see" numbers. Those are companies that decided their response system matters more than their forecast accuracy. Even the recovery side now requires operational readiness — companies that documented their exposure cleanly are recovering money. Companies that ran everything through one person's head are still trying to reconstruct what they paid.

The real cost of the Chief Everything Officer is not just slower growth. It is slower response to a market that is not going to slow down for you.

Bill Murphy, Founder & Chief Strategist · Colony Spark
Watch the Full Breakdown  →
 

FROM THE FLOOR

Black swans don't wait
for your planning cycle.

Jason Wong, Paking Duck, on stacked disruption in packaging

Jason Wong, founder and CEO of Paking Duck, put into words in a Supply Chain Dive interview what a lot of operators are feeling right now but struggling to articulate.

Packaging manufacturers and brands are getting hit from multiple directions at once: tariffs, metal duties, shipping disruption, and oil-driven material costs. Many brands feel they have exhausted their options and are now waiting to see what happens next. The disruptions are not arriving one at a time anymore — they are stacking on top of each other, shortening every planning window and punishing every slow response.

"These black swan events keep coming at us. We just don't have time to prepare."

Jason Wong

Founder & CEO, Paking Duck  ·  Supply Chain Dive, April 13, 2026

Wong's comment captures the emotional and operational truth of the moment. But it also points at the trap: "we don't have time to prepare" is what it feels like when preparation depends on one person making time in their calendar. Operators who have built response systems don't need to prepare in the moment — their systems already are prepared.

For manufacturers and distributors

If your response to each new disruption is a scramble from scratch, you're paying the founder-bottleneck tax. The work isn't to predict the next black swan. It's to build the decision infrastructure so the team can respond to whatever comes next without waiting for the calendar to open.

For vendors selling to manufacturers

Your customers are exhausted. They don't have mental space to onboard another vendor who shows up vague. The rep who walks in already knowing the last stated priority, the unresolved issue, and the commercial context wins the meeting. That's what The Stack this week is about.
 

THE STACK

The Post-Call Intelligence Agent.

Build memory into the workflow. Stop trusting memory itself.

No more lost commitments. No more tribal knowledge trapped in one person's inbox. The system carries context forward automatically.

The best operators are quietly building a layer between every important conversation and every next action. After a customer call, supplier check-in, plant review, or commercial meeting, the system takes the transcript and turns it into operating leverage. It extracts commitments, flags unresolved risk, updates the CRM or project tracker, and creates the next brief automatically.

Nobody has to trust memory. Nobody has to dig through notes three weeks later. The system carries context forward. In a stable market, dropped context is annoying. In a volatile market, dropped context gets expensive fast. If tariffs shift, a supplier slips, a customer changes volume, or a margin assumption moves, the companies that win are the ones that can reconnect today's conversation to last week's decision and next week's action without friction. That is the real use case. Not AI as novelty. AI as continuity.

What the agent does

After every important conversation, the system:

· Extracts commitments made by both sides, with deadlines and owners

· Flags unresolved risk or open questions that need escalation

· Updates the CRM or project tracker without human touch

· Creates the brief for the next conversation automatically

· Surfaces patterns across accounts — if five customers raise the same concern, leadership sees it early

For operators

Fewer missed follow-ups. Fewer handoff errors. Less tribal knowledge trapped in inboxes or in one person's head. And faster pattern recognition — when the same concern shows up across accounts or suppliers, leadership sees it earlier, not after the damage is done.

For vendors selling into manufacturing

Reps stop showing up vague. They walk in knowing the customer's last stated priority, the unresolved issue, the promised follow-up, and the commercial context. That changes the quality of the conversation immediately — and it changes how the customer perceives your team.

Step 1: Transcript ingestion — from Gong, Fathom, Otter, or Zoom

Step 2: Extraction agent — commitments, risks, decisions, open questions

Step 3: CRM connector — write commitments as action items against the account

The edge is not more activity. The edge is building memory into the workflow so the business becomes harder to knock off course. In a year like this, that is what being proactive actually looks like.
